The story makes sophisticated use of metaphor, particularly at the emotional climax when the narrator realizes how much his mother cherishes his presence. The physical remnants of the narrator's first visit—the washed mug placed back on the counter, the open book, the repositioned photograph, and the rationed blackberry jam—serve as an extended metaphor for the visit itself and the mother's unspoken affection. The narrator explicitly connects these objects to the abstract concept of the visit, realizing that "the visit had not ended when I got in the car. It had been sitting on her counter... while she kept it alive the only way she knew how, which was by using it, a little at a time, like a good thing." Furthermore, the story employs smaller, original metaphors throughout, such as describing the mother's stoic mindset as "the practical arithmetic of her kitchen" and noting that the drought-ridden county "had given up on its grass."
